match.reason: The new point is a broad list of wellbeing indicators (GDP per person, infant mortality, literacy, clean water, life satisfaction), which none of the bank points teach: the closest, geo-other-wellbeing-measures, is about the Multidimensional Poverty Index and the Happy Planet Index, and geo-gdp-per-person covers only GDP per person.

draft.title: Other measures of wellbeing
card: GDP per person
the value of all goods and services a country produces in a year, divided by its population. It is an economic measure of average income.
Infant mortality
the number of babies who die before their first birthday for every 1000 born alive. A high rate points to poor health care and living conditions.
Literacy
the share of adults who can read and write. It shows how well people have had access to education.
Other measures
Access to clean water shows the share of people with safe drinking water. Life satisfaction surveys ask people how happy they say they are with their lives.
draft.remember: Wellbeing can be measured by money, health, education, water and how people feel.

a.q: Which measure shows how people feel about their own lives?
a.why: Life satisfaction surveys ask people how happy they say they are, so they record feelings. GDP per person is tempting, but it measures average income, not how people feel.
a.clue: Which measure asks people a question?

b.q: Country X has a high GDP per person, but many babies there die before their first birthday. What does this suggest?
opts: Average income may hide poor health care
Average income shows health is also high
Literacy must also be very low there
b.why: GDP per person is an average income, so a country can have a high figure while many people lack good health care. A high infant mortality rate shows this gap. Infant mortality measures health, not education, and the case says nothing about literacy.
b.clue: One measure is about money and the other is about health.

b.best: Average income may hide poor health care

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may'). The wrong options use absolute words ('only', 'must') or overclaim, so a student can pick the answer from the wording without knowing the idea.

b.q: Country X has a high GDP per person, but many babies there die before their first birthday. What does this suggest?
opts: High average income does not guarantee good health care
High average income means health care is also good
Infant mortality measures education, not health
GDP per person measures the health of the population
